citation: Kolapo, A., & Didunyemi, A. J. Effects of exposure on adoption of agricultural smartphone apps among smallholder farmers in Southwest, Nigeria
population_and_technology: 380 smallholder farmers; agricultural smartphone apps
study_design: Cross-sectional survey with multistage sampling and counterfactual analysis
findings: Exposure was associated with higher app use; users showed higher productivity and technical-efficiency measures than comparison groups.
limitations: Non-random exposure and self-reported use limit causal interpretation; it studies adoption/productivity, not this calculator's comprehension or safety.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Direct Nigerian agriculture context; supports exposure, skills, and access risk framing.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Keep onboarding and labels explicit; do not infer app-specific comprehension or usefulness; future participant task study remains required.

citation: Ayim, C., Kassahun, A., Addison, C., & Tekinerdogan, B. Adoption of ICT innovations in the agriculture sector in Africa: a review of the literature
population_and_technology: African farmers and ICT services including mobile, text, voice, radio, and computers
study_design: Systematic literature review; 779 records and 23 primary studies
findings: Mobile services sought timely information, but adoption was constrained by poor infrastructure, policy gaps, and low user skills.
limitations: Literature published through 2019; heterogeneous technologies and limited product-level usability evidence.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Direct SSA agriculture context; supports low-skill, infrastructure, and channel assumptions.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Keep the app static and lightweight; retain low-bandwidth and literacy risks as explicit gates.

citation: Alant, B. P., & Bakare, O. O. A case study of the relationship between smallholder farmers’ ICT literacy levels and demographic data with respect to their use and adoption of ICT for weather forecasting
population_and_technology: Smallholder farmers; ICT literacy and use/adoption of ICT for weather forecasting
study_design: Case study using farmer ICT-literacy and demographic data
findings: ICT literacy and demographic characteristics were examined in relation to farmers’ use and adoption of ICT for weather forecasting.
limitations: South African case study and weather-information focus; no evaluation of this calculator or Nigerian users.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable SSA literacy and adoption context.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Use perceived usefulness and literacy as future outcomes to measure; do not claim them from literature.

citation: Chete, O., Koledoye, G., & Salami, R. The effectiveness of mobile phone utilisation for agricultural information dissemination among tomato farmers in Ondo State, Nigeria
population_and_technology: 100 tomato farmers; mobile phones and agricultural information
findings: Network problems and charging constraints were prominent; education and socioeconomic factors were associated with effective use.
limitations: Small local sample, self-report, and information-dissemination focus; no evaluation of this interface.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Direct Nigerian context for connectivity, charging, and literacy risks.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Treat low bandwidth, charging, and language as unresolved field risks; preserve offline-first behavior and test blocked-storage recovery.

citation: Ayanwale, A. B., & Kehinde, A. D. Determinants of use of digital innovation and its impact on land acquisition and food security among farming households in Nigeria
population_and_technology: 5,051 farming households; digital innovation and household outcomes
study_design: Secondary-data cross-sectional analysis using panel survey data
findings: Education, age, assets, financial access, and internet access were associated with digital innovation use; digital exclusion persisted despite mobile ownership.
limitations: Observational household-level associations do not establish app effects, comprehension, or safety.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Direct Nigerian context for unequal access and socioeconomic heterogeneity.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Do not assume smartphone ownership equals usable access; retain anonymous local calculation and defer user comprehension claims.

citation: Cheng, C., Beauchamp, A., Elsworth, G. R., & Osborne, R. H. Applying the Electronic Health Literacy Lens: systematic review of electronic health interventions targeted at socially disadvantaged groups
population_and_technology: Digital health interventions for socially disadvantaged groups
findings: User involvement and eHealth literacy were inconsistently addressed; interventions need attention to literacy, access, and the user's ability to find, understand, and act on information.
limitations: Health rather than agriculture; heterogeneous interventions and outcome measures.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable literacy and user-involvement context for low-literacy calculator copy.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Use plain language and visible explanations; require future comprehension testing rather than claiming the copy works.

citation: Hamilton, F. L., et al. Design and deployment of digital health interventions to reduce the risk of the digital divide
country_or_region: United Kingdom review with underserved-population evidence
population_and_technology: Adults affected by age, income, education, ethnicity, or digital exclusion; web/mobile interventions
findings: Co-development, iterative user testing, low-reading-age copy, images, human support, and affordable connectivity were recurring design/deployment themes.
limitations: Heterogeneous evidence, search through 2021, and few validated measures of digital-skill change.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable digital-divide requirements; not Nigerian farmer evidence.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Keep simple visible copy and defer translation; use browser checks as implementation evidence, not as user validation.

citation: Pavão, A. L. B., & Werneck, G. L. Health literacy in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review
country_or_region: LMICs, mostly Asia and Latin America
population_and_technology: Health-literacy studies in LMIC populations
study_design: Systematic review; 6,025 references and 36 included studies
findings: Definitions and measures varied; functional literacy was most common and broader literacy constructs were inconsistently used.
limitations: Health-literacy construct and measurement heterogeneity limit direct transfer to agricultural numeracy.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable warning against treating a single comprehension proxy as complete literacy evidence.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Map unit and ranking comprehension separately in any future participant study; no helpfulness proxy in this gate.

citation: McHenry, M. S., Fischer, L. J., Chun, Y., & Vreeman, R. C. A systematic review of portable electronic technology for health education in resource-limited settings
country_or_region: LMIC/resource-limited settings including Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania, India, Peru, Botswana, Thailand
population_and_technology: Portable devices with offline educational or decision-support content
study_design: Systematic review; 5,514 unique titles, 75 full texts, 10 included
findings: Offline portable resources were promising when culturally adapted and functional; technical support, cost, and theft were recurring limitations.
limitations: Only 10 included studies and largely health-education settings; positive findings do not validate this app.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable offline and cultural-adaptation evidence with some Nigerian coverage.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Retain offline calculation, no-egress behavior, and deferred physical-device validation; do not claim offline recovery in the field.

citation: Islam, M. S., et al. Mapping national ICT infrastructure to the requirements of potential digital health interventions in LMICs
population_and_technology: Digital-health infrastructure, policy, electricity, connectivity, and user access
study_design: JBI-informed scoping review and rapid-review synthesis; 118 studies plus contextual sources
findings: Interrupted electricity/internet, workforce, policy, affordability, and rural/gender access gaps shaped feasibility; context-specific tailoring was required.
limitations: Five-country health context is not Nigeria and includes contextual statistics alongside studies.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable LMIC infrastructure evidence.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Treat low bandwidth and power as design constraints; record browser evidence separately from physical-device evidence.

citation: ISO. ISO 9241-11:2018 Ergonomics of human-system interaction — Part 11: Usability: Definitions and concepts
population_and_technology: Interactive systems and products; specified users, goals, and context
findings: Usability is an outcome of use involving effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context; the standard does not prescribe a single method.
limitations: Paid standard and framework-level guidance; it supplies no population or product outcome.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Contextual usability definition; applicable to future calculator evaluation planning.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Separate effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction measures in future human validation; do not collapse them into a single literature claim.

citation: Nielsen, J. 10 usability heuristics for user interface design
population_and_technology: General software interfaces
findings: Visibility, match to the real world, error prevention, recognition over recall, and recoverable errors are relevant inspection lenses.
limitations: Practice guidance, not a controlled empirical study and not evidence of Nigerian farmer comprehension.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Useful inspection context but insufficient for population or product claims.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Use as a review checklist for labels, error messages, visible units, and recovery; require user testing for comprehension.

citation: Brooke, J. SUS — a quick and dirty usability scale
population_and_technology: Interactive systems; post-use questionnaire
findings: The System Usability Scale offers a short global usability measure for future comparative evaluation.
limitations: A global score cannot diagnose unit or ranking misunderstandings and requires actual users; the original chapter is not a Nigerian or agricultural study.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable evaluation instrument only; not active Stage 6 evidence.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: If participant validation is later authorized, pair task success and comprehension with SUS; do not use a SUS threshold now.

citation: Polson, P. G., Lewis, C., Rieman, J., & Wharton, C. Cognitive walkthroughs: a method for theory-based evaluation of user interfaces
population_and_technology: Task-based interface learning by exploration
findings: Cognitive walkthrough structures inspection around user goals, available actions, feedback, and whether a user can learn the next step.
limitations: Method validity depends on realistic task definitions and evaluators; inspection is not user performance evidence.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable method for calculator task-flow review.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Apply walkthrough prompts to crop selection, units, price range, ranking, print, reload, and error recovery; retain comprehension as unresolved.

citation: World Wide Web Consortium. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
population_and_technology: Web content and applications on desktop and mobile devices
findings: Perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles provide testable accessibility criteria across devices.
limitations: Conformance does not establish agricultural literacy, local-language adequacy, or actual assistive-technology success in this app.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable accessibility standard; product conformance is narrower than field usability.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Retain semantic labels, keyboard flows, contrast/axe checks, responsive tests, and future assistive-technology review.

citation: Page, M. J., et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews
population_and_technology: Systematic reviews and evidence syntheses
findings: PRISMA 2020 requires transparent objectives, eligibility, sources, search strategies, selection, synthesis, limitations, and flow reporting.
limitations: Designed primarily for systematic reviews; this rapid scoping review adapts it proportionately and does not claim a registered systematic review.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Contextual synthesis/reporting guidance.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Maintain the review question, exact strings, screening counts, source links, limitations, and explicit no-participant-validation statement.

citation: Pollock, D., et al. Scoping reviews, in the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis
population_and_technology: Scoping reviews across health and policy evidence
findings: JBI provides guidance on scoping-review questions, searching, selection, extraction, synthesis, and presentation of heterogeneous evidence.
limitations: Method guidance does not supply calculator evidence and the online manual is updated over time.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Contextual review-method guidance.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Use a broad mapping review and narrative synthesis; do not pool incomparable usability or adoption measures.

citation: Hong, Q. N., Gonzalez-Reyes, A., & Pluye, P. Improving the usefulness of the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool
population_and_technology: Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-method studies
study_design: Qualitative study of 20 MMAT users across eight countries
findings: MMAT usefulness depends on coverage, flexibility, learnability, and clear selection of appraisal criteria.
limitations: User interviews about the tool do not establish that MMAT classifications are objective or that the underlying evidence transfers to this product.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Contextual quality-appraisal method.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Record design-aware quality/context judgments per source instead of a pooled score or false precision.

citation: World Health Organization. Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions: a practical guide
population_and_technology: Digital health and mHealth interventions
findings: Evaluation should distinguish implementation fidelity, process measures, outcomes, context, and research questions across the intervention lifecycle.
limitations: Health-program guidance and not a product-specific usability validation; published in 2016.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Contextual evaluation-planning guidance.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Retain separate gates for browser behavior, physical-device behavior, participant comprehension, adoption, and forecast outcomes.

citation: Weirauch, V., Soehnchen, C., Burmann, A., & Meister, S. Methods, Indicators, and End-User Involvement in the Evaluation of Digital Health Interventions for the Public
country_or_region: International public end-user digital health studies
population_and_technology: Public-facing digital interventions and their evaluation methods
findings: Mixed methods, surveys, interviews, task/scenario tests, and active/qualitative end-user involvement were common; indicators and methods remained heterogeneous.
limitations: No formal quality appraisal by scoping-review design; health-focused evidence and publication/reporting bias limit transfer.
nigeria_lmic_relevance: Transferable evaluation-method evidence that reinforces the need for future users and explicit measures.
linked_calculator_requirement_or_test: Define future task, comprehension, satisfaction, and technical measures separately; do not replace them with the current literature gate.
